name: The sense of 'I' (ahaṃkāra)
description: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: One whose self is deluded by the sense of 'I' thinks 'I am the doer' while actions are done by the guṇas of prakṛti (3.27); the one who, without 'mine' and without 'I', has abandoned all desires attains peace (2.71).
antidotes: knowing the truth of the division of guṇas and actions (3.28)

name: Cavilling (asūyā)
description: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Those who cavil at Kṛṣṇa's teaching and do not follow it are deluded in all knowledge and lost; those who follow it without cavilling, with faith, are released (3.31–32).

name: Irresolution: the many-branched understanding
description: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The understandings of the irresolute are many-branched and endless, whereas resolute understanding is single (2.41); for those attached to enjoyment and power, carried away by the flowery speech of the ritual-minded, resolute understanding is not established in samādhi (2.44).

name: Desire (kāma)
description: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Desire arises from attachment to objects dwelt on and gives rise to anger (2.62); the ritual-minded are desire-souled (2.43); the one of steady wisdom gives up all desires (2.55, 2.71) and is not 'a desirer of desires' (2.70). Named with anger as the enemy born of rajas, all-devouring, covering knowledge as smoke covers fire, an insatiable fire, seated in the senses, mind and understanding (3.37–40).

name: The fault of faint-heartedness (kārpaṇya-doṣa)
description: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Arjuna says his very nature is struck by the fault of faint-heartedness and his mind bewildered about dharma, and so he asks for instruction (2.7). (In 2.49 those whose motive is the fruit are called kṛpaṇa, 'wretched'.)

name: Faintness, dejection (kaśmala)
description: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The dejection that came upon Arjuna at the critical moment: not practised by the noble, not leading to heaven, bringing disgrace (2.2).

name: Unmanliness and weakness of heart (klaibya, hṛdaya-daurbalya)
description: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Arjuna is told not to yield to unmanliness, which does not befit him, and to cast off petty weakness of heart and stand up (2.3).

name: Anger (krodha)
description: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Anger arises from desire and gives rise to delusion, confusion of memory, destruction of understanding and ruin (2.62–63); the sage of steady thought is free from it (2.56); with desire, born of rajas, it is the enemy (3.37).

name: Greed (lobha)
description: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: In Arjuna's argument, greed strikes down the minds of the Kauravas so that they do not see the fault in destroying the family (1.38), and his own side is ready to kill its own people from greed for the pleasures of kingship (1.45).

name: Hypocritical restraint (mithyācāra)
description: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: One who restrains the organs of action but sits dwelling in mind on sense-objects is called a hypocrite (3.6); contrasted with one who controls the senses by the mind and undertakes karma-yoga unattached (3.7).

name: Delusion, bewilderment (moha, saṃmoha)
description: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Arjuna's mind is bewildered about dharma (2.7); understanding must cross the thicket of delusion (2.52); delusion arises from anger and confuses memory (2.63); those deluded by the guṇas are attached to their actions (3.29); those who cavil are deluded in all knowledge (3.32); desire deludes the embodied one through the senses, mind and understanding (3.40). The one in the brahmic state is not bewildered (2.72).

name: Attraction and aversion (rāga-dveṣa)
description: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Attraction and aversion lie in the object of each sense; one should not come under their sway, for they are one's waylayers (3.34); the self-governed move among objects with senses free of them and attain serenity (2.64); the sage is free from passion, fear and anger (2.56).

name: Attachment (saṅga)
description: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Attachment arises from dwelling on objects and gives rise to desire (2.62); it is to be abandoned in action (2.48, 3.9) and is not to be directed to inaction (2.47); those attached to enjoyment and power lack resolute understanding (2.44); the ignorant are attached to action and to the actions of the guṇas (3.26, 3.29).

name: Grief (śoka)
description: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Arjuna's grief overwhelms him (1.47) and dries up his senses so that no kingdom could dispel it (2.8). Kṛṣṇa answers that the wise grieve neither for the dead nor the living (2.11) and repeatedly concludes 'you ought not to grieve' from the nature of the embodied self (2.25, 2.26, 2.27, 2.30).
antidotes: knowledge of the imperishable embodied self (2.11–30)

name: The turbulent senses (indriyāṇi pramāthīni)
description: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: The turbulent senses forcibly carry off the mind even of a discerning person who strives (2.60); the mind that follows the roving senses carries off wisdom as the wind a ship (2.67).

name: Despondency (viṣāda)
description: Bhagavad Gītā 1–3: Arjuna, overcome by pity and despairing on seeing his kin, describes his limbs failing, mouth drying, trembling, hair standing on end, the bow slipping, skin burning, inability to stand and a whirling mind (1.28–30; also 2.1, 2.10).
